newsitem.title: NORWAY: East Timor peace prize ends 1996 Nobel season.
newsitem.headline: East Timor peace prize ends 1996 Nobel season.

text.p: The prestigious Nobel Peace Prize went on Friday to two campaigners for East Timor independence, ending the eight-day 1996 Nobel season which began with a Polish poet receiving the literature award.

Bishop of East Timor Carlos Belo and resistance leader Jose Ramos-Horta were awarded the prize for their work to find a peaceful solution to the conflict on East Timor which has been in turmoil since Indonesia invaded it in 1975.
But the Nobel series ended on a tragic note with the announcement of the death of William Vickrey, a Canadian who shared the Nobel Prize for Economics just three days ago.

Vickrey, who was 82, died early on Friday after suffering a heart attack at the wheel of his car on Thursday night while driving to a conference in Boston, Massachusetts, a spokeswoman for Columbia University in New York said.

Belo and Ramos-Horta join a distinguished list of winners of a prize which since 1901 has gone to presidents, generals, pacifists, writers, religious leaders, revolutionaries and philosophers as well as, occasionally, institutions.

They will be able to attend the prize ceremony and candle-lit parade in Oslo on December 10, anniversary of the death of Swedish scientist Alfred Nobel, the inventor of dynamite, who founded the awards.
The other five Nobel awards are announced in Stockholm and presented in a glittering ceremony at the City Hall, also on December 10, which is the social event of Sweden's calendar.

This follows conditions stipulated in Nobel's 1895 will which stated the peace prize should be handled by Norway. No reason was given for the decision, which was taken at a time when Norway was in union with Sweden.
The peace prize was the last of six Nobel annual awards - all worth $1.12 million.
The annual awards began on October 3 with Polish poet and critic, Wislawa Szymborska, who received the Nobel Literature prize.
Szymborska, 73, described as the "Mozart of poetry", was the fifth pole or Polish-born writer to win the award.
The United States again dominated the four Nobel science awards, winning five out of 10 prizes, confirming a common view that U.S. colleges are producing the best scientific research.
Two Britons, one Canadian, an Australian and a Swiss also featured on the list.
U.S. physicists David Lee, Douglas Osheroff and Robert Richardson, won the 1996 physics prize for their quantum physics discovery on the superfluidity of the helium-3 isotope.
The trio made a breakthrough in low-temperature physics in the early 1970s at Cornell University in New York State.

Sweden's staid Royal Academy of Sciences took the unusual step of awarding the Nobel Chemistry Prize for a discovery made just 10 years ago, saying it may have a momentous effect on life in the next century.

American scientists Robert Curl and Richard Smalley and Briton Sir Harold Kroto won the award for the 1985 discovery of a form of the carbon element in the faceted shape of a soccer ball which they dubbed the "Buckminsterfullerene".
"Scientists should have discovered "fullerenes' 40 years ago but just didn't make the right calculations," Kroto said.

The medicine prize went to Australian Peter Doherty and Swiss Rolf Zinkernagel who discovered how the immune system recognises and can then kill infected cells, unlocking the mystery of how a vaccine needs to be composed.
The sixth award, economics, was added to the original list in 1968 to commemorate 300 years of the Swedish central bank.
This year it was awarded to Vickrey and British professor James Mirrlees, 60, for their individual "contribution to the economic theory of incentives under asymmetric information".
The two economists -- not widely known in the economic world -- had never met even though jointly their work sowed the seeds of a new branch in economic theory.
